newsitem.title: NEPAL: South Asian trade negotiators begin talks in Nepal.
newsitem.headline: South Asian trade negotiators begin talks in Nepal.

text.p: Negotiators from South Asian nations on Friday began talks on tariff cuts intended to boost trade in the region, officials said on Friday.

"This is an effort to go into significant tariff cuts in order to make SAPTA (South Asian Preferential Trading Agreement) an effective vehicle to increase intra-regional trade in South Asia," an official of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) said.

He said the meeting would also end the second round of negotiations on trade liberalisation under SAPTA, which allows concessional trade among the seven SAARC countries under the first round concluded last year.
Ashok K. Attri, director of the Kathmandu-based SAARC secretariat, told Reuters the current round of negotiations had a two-pronged objective.
"Negotiators will enlarge the schedule of concessions by widening the list of items and deepen tariff cuts both on the existing and new products," Attri said.
Member countries of SAPTA have agreed on a list of 226 items for tariff concessions. The least-developed member countries are entitled to additional tariff concessions.

SAARC was formed in December 1985 to improve the economies of the more than one-fifth of the world's population that lives in South Asia. It groups Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.
SAPTA, whose member countries provide tariff concessions for imports from within the region, was incorporated within the SAARC framework in 1993 and came into force in December 1995.

Negotiators said they would concentrate on bilateral talks and complete the consolidated schedule of concessions. This will eventually be forwarded to the SAARC Council of Ministers, which is comprised of members' foreign ministers and is scheduled to meet on December 19 in New Delhi for implemention.
Diplomats said implementation would be a major step towards realising the goal set by the SAARC of launching the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) before 2005.
"The significant contribution of this meeting will be remembered by all as an important milestone in this regard," said Secretary General Naeem U Hasan, SAARC's top bureaucrat.
Officials said SAPTA would help increase the trade between the seven South Asian nations, which currently represents only 3.4 percent of total global trade.
